Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Therapy

Contact UsSee Practitioners

When Your Mind and Body Still React as Though Danger Has Not Passed

Perhaps weeks, months, or even years have passed since a distressing event, yet your nervous system still feels locked on high alert.

Maybe unexpected memories, vivid nightmares, or sudden surges of panic and physical tension interrupt your day without warning. Or perhaps you find yourself steering clear of certain places, conversations, crowds, or thoughts, working hard just to keep difficult feelings at bay.

You may have wondered why you cannot simply "move on" or feel settled again, even when you logically know you are safe right now.

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a recognised clinical response that can develop after experiencing, witnessing, or being repeatedly exposed to frightening, threatening, or deeply distressing events.

If these experiences feel familiar, you do not have to manage them on your own.

With paced, evidence-based psychological support, it is possible to build present-day grounding and work through the impact of PTSD at a rhythm that prioritises your safety.

Could This Be What You're Experiencing?

PTSD affects people differently depending on their history, support network, and the nature of what they experienced. Symptoms generally fall across intrusive experiences, avoidance, changes in mood or thinking, and heightened physical alertness.

You may notice that you:

  • experience unwanted, distressing memories, flashbacks, or nightmares related to a past event
  • feel intense emotional distress or physical reactions, such as a racing heart, sweating, or shaking, when reminded of what happened
  • actively avoid places, people, activities, conversations, or thoughts connected to the experience
  • feel constantly watchful, tense, easily startled, or unable to let your guard down (hypervigilance)
  • struggle to fall asleep, stay asleep, or feel rested due to alertness or disturbing dreams
  • notice difficulty concentrating, memory gaps, or feeling mentally foggy during everyday tasks
  • feel emotionally numb, detached from loved ones, or unable to experience positive emotions easily
  • carry persistent feelings of guilt, shame, anger, or negative beliefs about yourself or the world
  • feel irritable or experience sudden surges of frustration or overwhelm in everyday situations

Experiencing distress after a frightening event is a natural human response, and early reactions often settle with time and support. When these patterns persist beyond a month and disrupt daily life, a clinically informed assessment can help clarify whether PTSD or another stress-related concern is contributing.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Every person reaches out for PTSD support at a different stage.

You may be seeking help because:

  • distressing memories, nightmares, or triggers are disrupting your sleep, work, or daily routines
  • staying constantly on guard has left you physically and emotionally exhausted
  • avoidance is shrinking your world, making driving, social outings, or everyday activities feel difficult
  • irritability, emotional numbness, or withdrawal is straining your closest relationships
  • you have experienced a transport accident, workplace incident, medical emergency, assault, natural disaster, or repeated occupational exposure
  • you have spoken with your GP about a Mental Health Treatment Plan and want a practitioner experienced in trauma-focused care

You do not need to have everything worked out, or be ready to recount every detail, before reaching out.

Understanding PTSD

Why the Threat Response Stays Active

During a traumatic or life-threatening event, the brain's survival system shifts into immediate protection mode, releasing stress hormones and storing sensory fragments of the experience so you can recognise future danger quickly.

In PTSD, that memory-filing process can remain incomplete. Instead of being stored as an event that happened in the past, reminders in the present can trigger the brain and body to react as though the threat is happening right now.

This is a physiological survival response, not a sign of weakness, fragility, or failure to cope.

Evidence-based PTSD therapies focus on helping your nervous system regain a sense of present-day safety and gradually process traumatic memories so they lose their immediate emotional and physical charge.

When PTSD Affects Everyday Life

PTSD can influence several areas of daily functioning simultaneously.

Sleep and Nighttime Rest

Difficulty switching off, hyper-awareness of sounds at night, and distressing dreams often lead to chronic fatigue that affects the following day.

Concentration and Everyday Decisions

When much of your mental energy goes toward scanning for potential triggers or managing internal distress, focus, memory, and planning can feel noticeably harder.

Sense of Safety and Mobility

Routine activities, such as driving, going to busy shops, attending appointments, or being in unfamiliar spaces, may feel overwhelming or exhausting.

Emotional Regulation and Mood

Alternating between heightened tension, sudden irritability, and emotional shutdown can leave you feeling disconnected from yourself.

Self-Perception and Trust

Trauma can shift how you view yourself, other people, and the predictability of the world, often fostering self-blame or caution around trusting others.

Everyone's experience of PTSD is unique, and therapy is always tailored around your specific comfort level and clinical needs.

When PTSD Affects Relationships and Family

Navigating Connection While Carrying Trauma

When you are working hard internally just to feel steady, staying emotionally present with partners, children, or friends can feel challenging.

Loved ones may notice you pulling back, seeming distant, or reacting strongly to small stressors, without understanding what is happening beneath the surface.

Over time, this can contribute to:

  • feeling disconnected, numb, or unable to share what you are going through
  • avoiding family outings, social gatherings, or crowded environments
  • heightened tension, irritability, or misunderstandings at home
  • partners or family members feeling unsure how to support you without accidentally triggering distress
  • feeling isolated even when surrounded by people who care

Recognising these patterns is not about blame: it creates space for clearer communication and paced, supportive care.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Structured, Safety-First Support Tailored to You

Evidence-based PTSD therapy is collaborative, transparent, and paced around your readiness. You remain in control of the process at every stage, and memory-focused work only begins once practical grounding and safety tools are in place.

Depending on your individual needs and goals, therapy may focus on:

  • building practical nervous system grounding and stabilisation skills for managing triggers and distress
  • understanding how PTSD symptoms and trauma reminders operate in daily life
  • gently processing traumatic memories using established, evidence-based approaches when you feel ready
  • exploring unhelpful beliefs around safety, guilt, trust, and self-blame
  • rebuilding confidence in everyday routines, sleep habits, and avoided activities
  • strengthening communication and boundaries within family and close relationships

Support moves at a pace that respects your wellbeing and clinical stability throughout.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

With tailored, evidence-based psychological support, many adults gradually experience greater steadiness and freedom in everyday life.

Depending on your individual goals and circumstances, therapy may help you:

  • feel more grounded and settled in the present moment when reminders arise
  • experience fewer or less intense intrusive memories, flashbacks, and nightmares
  • gradually re-engage with meaningful activities, places, and routines
  • support steadier sleep habits and daytime energy
  • respond to stress and triggers with practical calming strategies
  • build clearer communication and connection with partners, family, or colleagues

Progress is individualised and rarely linear, and a supportive therapeutic relationship provides consistent guidance along the way.

Small Changes Can Make Everyday Life More Manageable

Practical Grounding Steps Alongside Therapy

When your nervous system feels on alert, simple present-moment anchors can help remind your body that you are safe right now.

Alongside professional support, many adults find it helpful to:

  • orient to your current surroundings, naming objects in the room, noticing the date, or feeling your feet firmly on the floor, when memories intrude
  • practise slow, steady breathing with a longer exhale to help settle physical tension
  • create a calm, predictable wind-down routine before sleep with dim lighting and minimal stimulating news or screens
  • keep a brief grounding kit nearby (such as a textured object, cold water, or a calming scent) for high-stress moments
  • plan gentle transitions and buffer time before and after demanding appointments or busy environments
  • remind yourself that reactions are protective habits, approaching difficult moments with patience rather than self-criticism

Strategies work best when adapted to your comfort level, environment, and personal preferences.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Care for Adults

Because PTSD affects both mind and body, care is tailored around your history, clinical presentation, and personal preferences.

Evidence-Based PTSD Psychological Therapy

Depending on your practitioner's training and your goals, established approaches, such as Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (TF-CBT), Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), Prolonged Exposure, or phased stabilisation approaches, may help support processing and recovery.

Coping Skills and Routine Support

Sessions can incorporate practical tools for sleep hygiene, trigger management, and pacing daily responsibilities safely.

GP, Specialist, and Multidisciplinary Support

Your General Practitioner (GP) can discuss a Mental Health Treatment Plan where eligible, coordinate referrals (including under WorkCover, motor accident, or veteran schemes where applicable), and explore whether medical review or broader healthcare support may be appropriate alongside psychological care.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Taking the First Step Without Pressure

Reaching out for PTSD support can feel difficult, especially if talking about the past feels overwhelming or you are unsure which therapy approach suits you best.

You do not need to share details of the traumatic event during your initial enquiry, nor do you need to have everything worked out before contacting us.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our team listens respectfully to what you feel comfortable sharing, explains available pathways clearly, and helps match you with an appropriately trained practitioner.

Whether you are:

  • exploring support for recent or long-standing post-traumatic stress symptoms
  • looking for a practitioner trained in EMDR or trauma-focused therapies
  • holding a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan or insurance-related referral
  • wanting in-person sessions in Brisbane or private online appointments from home

we are here to help make taking that first step feel safe, respectful, and manageable.

Why Clients Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With You at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administration Services (MBP) provides a welcoming, neutral, and professionally managed entry point for adults seeking psychological and allied health care.

Clinically Informed Intake

Sensitive, respectful intake processes help us understand your preferences and identify a suitable support pathway.

Appropriate Practitioner Matching

We connect you with clinical psychologists, general psychologists, social workers, or counsellors whose training and scope of practice align with PTSD and trauma-focused care.

Coordinated Care

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can liaise with your GP, psychiatrist, and other health professionals involved in your care.

Practical Referral Support

Our team assists with GP referral requirements, Mental Health Treatment Plans, and Medicare-related paperwork where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available at our Brisbane clinics in Toowong and Manly West, alongside secure Online Therapy / Telehealth Australia-wide where clinically appropriate.

Start with a Conversation

You Don't Have to Carry Post-Traumatic Stress Alone

You may not be sure which therapy approach is right for you, or how to begin talking about what you have been experiencing.

If lingering distress, triggers, or hypervigilance continue to make everyday life harder than it should be and you would like steady, non-judgmental support, reaching out can be a helpful first step.

Share only as much as feels comfortable, and our team will help you explore an appropriate pathway forward.

Contact Michelle Barratt Psychology on (07) 3185 0040 or reach out via our online contact form to learn more about trauma and PTSD therapy support.
